title: Taliban Reportedly Bars Women's Names From Records in Afghan Province
excerpt: Officials and healthcare workers in Balkh province have reportedly been told to replace women's first names with the generic 'Bibi' in documents, medical records and prescriptions, with activists reporting degrading animal labels in some cases.
body:
• Authorities in Afghanistan's northern Balkh province have reportedly ordered officials and healthcare workers to stop using women's first names in official documents, medical records and prescriptions, according to reporting by Spain's El País.
  • Women are instead to be addressed as "Bibi", a generic term meaning grandmother or old woman; activists say some women have also been called by degrading animal names such as "goat" or "cow".
  • Activists warn that filing medical records under identical generic names raises the risk of treatment errors, and that local bans in Afghanistan have previously been expanded nationwide.
  • The report is based on testimony gathered by El País from women, doctors and activists; the Taliban has not publicly confirmed the Balkh order in the reporting.

The Taliban have reportedly banned the use of women's names in official documents in Afghanistan's northern Balkh province, extending the erasure to medical records and prescriptions, according to a report by Spain's El País carried by Fox News and other outlets.

Healthcare workers and other public employees have been instructed to address women as "Bibi", meaning grandmother or old woman, according to reporting by the Afghan news outlet Zan Times and The Guardian cited by El País. The order reportedly applies to hospitals, private clinics and other public offices in Balkh.

"The first step to dehumanising a person"

Afghan women's rights activist Lalah Osmany, who is based in Germany, told El País that testimony from women, doctors and civil rights activists indicates some women are also being referred to in degrading terms such as "goat" or "cow".

"This is a systematic process of dehumanisation. When a regime replaces a woman's name and gives her one of an animal, it is stripping her of her human soul and reducing her to a mere biological creature or the property of a man."

— Lalah Osmany, Afghan women's rights activist, to El País

Osmany also warned that the naming ban could endanger patients: if prescriptions and medical records are filed under identical generic names, the risk of medical errors rises. An Afghan activist speaking under a pseudonym confirmed the reported order to El País, although she said it had so far been ignored in her area, a reminder that enforcement of Taliban directives often varies between localities.

A practice older than the Taliban, now reportedly made law

The avoidance of women's first names in public is rooted in tribal traditions that treat pronouncing a woman's name publicly as an affront to male honour, The Business Standard reported in its account of the El País investigation. The custom reaches wedding invitations and tombstones, where women are often identified only as the wife or daughter of a male relative. Activists say it is a cultural tradition rather than an Islamic requirement. Under the US-backed government that preceded the Taliban's return to power in 2021, the taboo persisted socially, but there was no legal prohibition on using women's names: they appeared on passports, and women could work and campaign publicly under their own names.

Osmany has campaigned against that erasure since 2017, when she launched the #WhereIsMyName campaign calling for mothers' names to be included on official documents, including their children's birth certificates. In September 2020 the campaign won a legal breakthrough when the government approved the voluntary inclusion of women's names on children's birth certificates. "A nameless person cannot dream, cannot own property, cannot claim justice, nor be remembered in history," she said.

Why a provincial order matters

Zubaida Akbar, who directs the Afghanistan programme at the women's rights organisation Femena, warned that the Taliban could eventually impose the ban nationwide, citing previous instances in which local restrictions were expanded across the country. Femena has counted more than 144 decrees restricting Afghan women's rights since the Taliban returned to power in August 2021, according to El País. Women have been shut out of most professions and subjected to restrictions on speaking in public, and some have resorted to running underground businesses and secret schools, according to Associated Press reporting published on November 17.

The practical consequences reach beyond symbolism. Activists say a name missing from official documents can block a woman in family disputes as well as in hospitals: exiled journalist Khadija Amín was excluded from her children's birth certificates under traditional customs, and when her former husband took their three children to Germany in 2024, German police were initially unable to process her custody complaint because she lacked official documents establishing her legal identity as their mother.

Whether Balkh's reported order is enforced, ignored, or extended is now the question Afghan activists are watching. The Taliban authorities have not publicly confirmed the directive in the reporting published so far. this article will be updated if they respond.
